tldr: Using a passive dynamic walker as a model, this study mathematically reveals why adding "softness" (compliance) to a robot eases control, analyzing phase space geometry and information metrics in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS).
hero_caption: Conceptual diagram of the dynamic model of a passive walker and its viable region in phase space. It illustrates how the range of states permitting sustained walking and the distribution of trajectories change depending on the slope angle $\gamma$ and ankle compliance.
overview:
Robotics has long possessed the intuitive knowledge that "having a soft body makes control easier." This concept is known as "morphological computation," where the body itself takes over part of the computation. However, almost no theories have rigorously and quantitatively explained from the perspectives of information theory and dynamical systems why softness reduces the controller's burden.

The authors tackled this mystery using a model of an unpowered "passive dynamic walker" walking down a slope, equipped with a compliant joint. Previously, it was roughly assumed that control becomes easier because the volume of the phase space (state space) permitting sustained walking shrinks. However, the authors uncovered a crucial insight: the phase space "volume itself (geometric support)" and the "probability distribution (measure)" with which states visit that space under dynamics are two entirely different things.

To verify this, they incorporated a spring element into a double-pendulum-type compass-gait walker and conducted Monte Carlo simulations accounting for rigorous heel-strike ground collision dynamics. Furthermore, they introduced a novel metric called "RKHS distribution complexity" that evaluates the dispersion of state probability distributions using a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS).

As a result, they mathematically proved that introducing compliance actually does not reduce the "viable volume" in the task space at all. Instead, compliance allows excess mechanical energy to be distributed and absorbed into internal springs, causing the task space states to concentrate strongly in lower-energy regions. In other words, softness does not shrink the "range of possible states"; rather, it "tightens the distribution of states," thereby reducing the effective amount of information the controller must handle.
contributions: Mathematically proved that the essence of compliance facilitating control lies not in shrinking the volume of the viable region, but in concentrating the task-state probability distribution toward lower energies.

Proposed "RKHS distribution complexity," a new information-geometric metric using reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) to integrate the geometric "support (volume)" of phase space with the dynamically induced "probability measure."

Quantified via Monte Carlo methods how ankle springs affect the viable region and information complexity in a hybrid dynamical system incorporating rigorous passive walker heel-strike collision dynamics.

sections.heading: Capturing the Link Between Embodiment and Intelligence with Mathematics
sections.summary: Explains the motivation of this study based on the concept of embodied cognition, where body structure and dynamics shape intelligence and control. It aims to quantitatively formulate the effect of morphological computation—often discussed qualitatively—as a relationship between information metrics and dynamical systems.
sections.details:
In the fields of robotics and artificial intelligence, as exemplified by the work of Rolf Pfeifer and others, there has long been a discussion that "intelligence and meaning emerge from embodied agents interacting with their environment." The phenomenon where physical dynamical properties take over the computation of actuators and brains is termed "morphological computation" and is highly compelling.

However, most previous discussions remained conceptual and qualitative. It was extremely difficult to predict with mathematical formulas how physical compliance directly relates to an agent's information-processing capability and computational load.

This study narrows its focus onto this ambitious theme, aiming to quantitatively unravel why the "softness/compliance" observed in robots and biological bodies aids control through rigorous mathematical modeling. Providing design guidelines for hybrid robots that combine rigid skeletons with compliant elements is a major goal of this work.

sections.heading: Equations Connecting Mind and Body: What Is the Microscopic State Count $W$ of Phase Space?
sections.summary: Introduces the foundational equations connecting the complexity of a control program (a metric of the mind) and the robot's dynamical system (a metric of the body). It extends the concept of entropy from statistical mechanics, presenting the idea that the phase space volume $W$ accessible to the dynamical system dictates the length of the control program.
sections.details:
The central idea for connecting the mind (control system) and body (dynamics) is importing the concept of entropy from statistical mechanics into dynamical systems. Even in systems with an immense number of microscopic degrees of freedom, entropy allows a bridge to a small set of observable variables and macroscopic behavior.

The authors postulate the "Mind–Body Nexus equations," which state that across a broad class of dynamical systems satisfying Shannon–Kolmogorov (S-K) axioms, the expected length (complexity) of a control program is tied to the number of accessible microscopic states (or phase space volume) $W$ within the phase space. Phase space is the space listing all states of the system, such as positions and velocities.

The key point here is that $W$ is not merely an abstract number; it represents "how widely the trajectories permitted by the system's equations of motion spread out." In a deterministic dynamical system devoid of quantum-mechanical path hysteresis or history dependence, the elegant relationship between Boltzmann entropy and Shannon entropy holds directly. In short, if the body's structure can constrain the search range $W$ in phase space, the complexity of the program that the controller needs to learn or compute can be fundamentally reduced.

sections.heading: Ultimate Morphological Computation: Adding Ankle Compliance to a Passive Walker
sections.summary: Adopts an unpowered passive walker descending a slope as a model and analyzes its phase space. Beginning with the simplest walker, it formulates how mechanical energy and state space change when compliant spring elements are added to the joints.
sections.details:
The most iconic example demonstrating the power of morphological computation is the "passive dynamic walker." Completely devoid of actuators, it continues to walk down a slope smoothly like a human relying solely on physical geometry, gravity, and floor collisions. Because the body itself strongly constrains the motion, it can walk with zero control from a brain (controller).

### IV-A The Simplest Ruina–Garcia Walker
The baseline model is the "simplest walker (Garcia et al. model)," featuring a point mass at the hip, massless legs, and point feet. Here, an inelastic heel-strike collision law holds, allowing the viable domain of phase space where walking does not collapse to be derived in an analytically closed form.

### IV-B Joint Compliance and Foot Rocker Effects
Next, compliance (internal coordinate $\phi$) is added to this model's joints. Introducing a compliant joint with spring constant $k$ (torsional spring) and moment of inertia $J$ immediately expands the phase space describing the motion to 4 dimensions.

Under a small-deflection approximation, the energy gains the spring's elastic potential energy $\frac{1}{2}k\phi^2$ and kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}J\dot{\phi}^2$. Adding compliance mitigates impact-induced collision losses and reshapes the viable state space. Furthermore, adopting circular arc feet (rocker feet) also alters the continuation conditions after collisions, as captured mathematically.

captions.F1: The viable domain in the leg phase space of the passive walker (relationship between angle $\theta$ and angular velocity $\omega$). It shows that mechanical energy conservation and geometric constraints strongly confine the accessible states inside an elliptical boundary.

sections.heading: Analysis of the Compass Gait: Volume Stays the Same, but the "Distribution" Changes!
sections.summary: Examines a compass-gait walker with uniform-rod legs, calculating velocity resets due to collisions and the admissible phase space. Here, the paper proves the core finding: adding compliance does not shrink the task-space volume (support) permitting walking, but instead alters the internal probability distribution.
sections.details:
For a two-legged compass walker with uniform rod-like mass distributions, the paper rigorously derives the swing leg position, Jacobian matrix, and discontinuous velocity reset laws at touchdown (heel strike) from the leg angle coordinates $q=[q_1, q_2]^T$.

### V-A & B Post-Impact Viable Set and Complexity Bounds
Evaluating the set of states that can sustain walking after an impact (post-impact viable set) $D^+$ using Monte Carlo methods determines the extent of the viable region according to slope angle $\alpha$. This phase space volume $W$ provides an upper bound on Shannon entropy and, consequently, control complexity.

### V-C & D True Effects of Compliance: Support Geometry and Induced Measure
This is the most exciting theoretical development in the paper! Let $D_r$ be the viable domain of task variables (angles and velocities directly related to walking) for the rigid walker, and let $D_c$ be the viable domain for the system with an added compliant joint $\eta$.

When the Hamiltonian is separable into task and compliant systems, the compliant joint can assume a zero-energy equilibrium point ($\eta=0$). Consequently, projecting the 4D viable domain $D_c$ onto the task variable space $\Pi_x D_c$ yields a region that perfectly matches the original rigid domain $D_r$ ($\Pi_x D_c = D_r$). In other words, "adding compliance does not shrink the size of the viable region in task space (support geometry) by even a millimeter."

### V-E Impact on Information Complexity: From Volume to Probability Measure
Why, then, does compliance facilitate control? The answer lies in the "probability measure." Even though the accessible range (support) remains identical, the frequency/density distribution $P(x)$ with which the dynamics visits that space shifts drastically. Because the extra degrees of freedom absorb energy, task states are naturally drawn toward low-energy regions. Therefore, looking solely at the scalar volume $W$ is merely a zeroth-order rough approximation; measuring the true control complexity requires a new framework capable of capturing the "bias in the distribution."

captions.F3: Variation of the viable phase space volume $W(\gamma)$ with respect to slope angle $\gamma$, accounting for rigorous heel-strike collision resets. As the slope steepens, energy supplied by gravity increases, showing a monotonic increase in the volume of states that can sustain walking.

sections.heading: Monte Carlo Simulation: Compliance Concentrates States Toward Low Energy
sections.summary: Conducts numerical simulations using Monte Carlo methods across three walker models. It numerically demonstrates that compliance biases the state probability density toward the lower-energy side, and that the heel-strike impact dynamics themselves discontinuously contract the phase space volume.
sections.details:
To substantiate the theory, the authors compared three models: a rigid compass walker, a walker with a compliant joint, and a compliant walker with distributed mass and foot dynamics. In each simulation, $10^5$ samples drawn uniformly from the admissible energy region were used to determine post-impact viability.

### VI-B Effect of Compliance on Task State Distribution
Analyzing with a local quadratic energy model, states in the 2D rigid model are uniformly distributed inside the energy ellipse. In this case, the normalized expected energy value is $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5$.

However, when sampling uniformly in the 4D model with an added compliant joint and projecting onto the task space (2D), the total expected energy in the 4D space is $\frac{2}{3}$. Because half of it is allocated to the task system, the expected task-system energy drops significantly to $\frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333$. In the simulation, this closely matched theory at approximately 0.334, confirming that the probability mass concentrates tightly near the origin (low-energy states) while retaining the full width of the support (viable range).

### VI-C Impact of Heel-Strike Dynamics
Furthermore, the heel-strike phenomenon where the foot impacts the ground acts as a powerful filter geometrically contracting phase space. At a slope angle of $\alpha=0.3\,\mathrm{rad}$, a single collision dissipates roughly 32% ($1 - \cos^2(2\alpha) \approx 0.319$) of the kinetic energy associated with angular velocity. The phase space area contraction rate computed from the coordinate Jacobian also reaches approximately 17.5%. It is evident that the passive dynamic phenomenon of collisions itself narrows down the state space to prevent the robot from diverging.

sections.heading: Information Geometry via RKHS: Measuring the True Complexity
sections.summary: Constructs a distribution embedding framework using RKHS to describe both viable domain "volume" and dynamically induced "probability distributions" in a unified manner. It demonstrates that compliance concentrates the spectrum of the covariance operator, dramatically reducing true complexity for the controller.
sections.details:
If the volume is the same but the probability distributions differ, how should one measure complexity? The authors introduced "reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS)" and "kernel mean embeddings," widely used in machine learning.

### VII-A to D Kernel Embeddings and Induced Geometry
A probability measure $P$ on the state space is represented via a feature map as a mean embedding $\mu_P = \int k(\cdot, x) dP(x)$ in a Hilbert space. As a result, even if two distributions share the same geometric support, differing distributions can be distinctly differentiated in the Hilbert space. Furthermore, defining a Riemannian metric pulled back from the Fubini–Study metric allows the distinctiveness of states in the feature space to be measured geometrically.

### VII-E Definition of RKHS Distribution Complexity
Defining the centered covariance operator of the probability measure $P$ as $C_P$, the authors defined "RKHS distribution complexity" using a Fredholm determinant as $\mathcal{C}(P) = \log\det_F(I + \gamma C_P) = \sum_i \log(1 + \gamma \lambda_i)$, where $\lambda_i$ are the eigenvalues of $C_P$. When the dynamical system moves only in a few independent directions, eigenvalues concentrate into specific components, shrinking this complexity $\mathcal{C}(P)$.

### VII-F Striking Contrast in Numerical Experiments
Calculations on a quadratic passive walker model ($N_s=300$ samples, 20 runs) yielded striking results:
- Standard Euclidean volume $W_{\mathrm{Euc}}$: roughly $4.189$ for both rigid and compliant models
- RKHS pullback geometric volume $W_K$: roughly $6.155$ for both rigid and compliant models
- RKHS distribution complexity $\mathcal{C}(P)$: significantly dropped from $48.25$ in the rigid model down to $38.99$ in the compliant model!

While the geometric volumes ($W_{\mathrm{Euc}}$ and $W_K$) did not change at all, compliance biased states toward lower energies, reducing the effective rank of the covariance operator and dramatically lowering only the distribution complexity $\mathcal{C}(P)$. The essence of softness facilitating control emerged clearly in numerical form.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Outlook: Softness as Information Processing Through the Body
sections.summary: Discusses the importance of reframing morphological computation as a dual mechanism of "state space reduction" and "reorganization of probability distributions." Notes that the proposed theory applies broadly to embodied AI, including manipulation and reinforcement learning, beyond just bipedal walking.
sections.details:
The findings of this study offer an exquisitely refined new interpretation of the long-debated morphological computation hypothesis. Morphology does not merely "physically restrict the range of motion via physical walls." Its true role lies in "cleverly reorganizing the probability distribution of dynamically generated trajectories within the permissible space."

From this perspective, the computational relief experienced by the controller (brain) should be understood not through the zeroth-order metric of phase space volume, but as an information-geometric structure captured by RKHS distribution complexity. By adding just a single spring to an ankle, the variance of states observed by the controller is suppressed, effectively shrinking the search space required for learning and feedback control.

This theory is not limited to passive walkers. It applies to any system where the body and dynamics produce probability distributions, including manipulation with compliant robot arms, soft robotics, co-optimization of body and policy in reinforcement learning, and biological motor control systems. Future work is expected to quantitatively link this theoretical complexity $\mathcal{C}(P)$ directly to real controller computation time, memory usage, and control energy.

sections.heading: Appendix: Complex Geometry, the Bergman Kernel, and the Path to Musculoskeletal Robots
sections.summary: Explains mathematical details for calculating phase space volume (constructing reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces with the Bergman kernel) and discusses applications to the musculoskeletal humanoid robot "Ecce" developed in an EU project.
sections.details:
The appendix outlines the background of mathematical tools used in the main text along with advanced computational methods.

### Volume Computation via the Bergman Kernel and Coherent States
In phase spaces with extremely complicated boundaries, such as those arising from stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) or nonlinear dynamical systems, obtaining volume via ordinary coordinate integration is challenging. To address this, the authors present an elegant geometric method: mapping the classical state space to "coherent states" on a Hilbert space using a weighted Bergman kernel from complex geometry, and computing the volume through Riemann mapping and integration of the kernel's diagonal elements.

### Connection to the Musculoskeletal Robot "Ecce"
While the passive walker is constructed from rigid links, it fully leverages the principles of morphological computation. What happens, then, in an actual musculoskeletal robot driven by compliant tendon mechanisms? The appendix introduces "Ecce," a tendon-driven humanoid robot developed in an EU project in which the authors participated. Even for complex robots with countless elastic elements (artificial muscles and tendons) like Ecce, the equations in this paper open a path to quantitatively designing which joints should possess what degree of compliance to minimize the burden on the brain (control program).

captions.F4: The tendon-driven musculoskeletal humanoid robot "Ecce" developed under the EU project "ECCEROBOT." It is cited as a prime example where compliant tendon structures embedded across the entire body perform morphological computation, dynamically reducing the computational burden of complex whole-body control.

takeaways: The true reason "compliance aids control" is not that it reduces the volume of admissible motion, but that it concentrates the task-space state probability distribution toward lower energies.

Quantitatively evaluating morphological computation requires not just phase space volume (support), but the RKHS distribution complexity $\mathcal{C}(P)$, which assesses the dynamically induced "probability measure."

A mathematical foundation has been established to optimize where and what compliance (spring stiffness) should be placed in robot mechanical design, guided by information theory and controller computational load.
limitations: The proposed RKHS distribution complexity $\mathcal{C}(P)$ is an information-geometric structural metric; its direct correspondence with real controller execution time (CPU cycles), memory consumption, and electrical power consumption has not been empirically validated.

Most analytical models assume a small-deflection quadratic energy approximation (locally linear springs), leaving open the question of whether this directly generalizes to soft materials with large deformations and strong nonlinear viscoelasticity.
In high-dimensional, stochastic complex systems, computing reachable sets and RKHS covariance operators for rigorous hybrid dynamical systems incurs high numerical computational costs.
